newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambia politics fail to match economic reforms.
newsitem.headline: Zambia politics fail to match economic reforms.

text.p: Zambia is pursuing economic reform policies which could make it a model in a continent littered with failure, but political liberalisation is failing to keep pace and western donors are losing interest, analysts say.
Its supporters include the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund -- unusual allies in Africa, where reform programmes often stall and promises are regularly broken.
President Frederick Chiluba won a landslide in controversial elections held last November despite an opposition boycott.

His main rival, former president and "father of the nation" Kenneth Kaunda, was kept out of the vote by a new law which donor countries said had rolled back many of the democratic gains Zambia enjoyed following years of one-party rule.

Western donors and Japan cut off balance of payments support last year, although analysts said funding might have been resumed if economic reform had stayed on track and Chiluba had showed renewed commitment to democratic principles.
But a clampdown on the opposition, and on civic groups and the media makes it almost certain that aid will be withheld.
"The government has made it extremely difficult for the donor community to help it," one Western diplomat said.
"Most Western governments are agreed that the conditions necessary for a resumption of normal aid flows have not been fulfilled."
Last year's state budget was 1,161.6 billion kwacha ($893 million), with 36 percent of it coming from donors.
A freeze in aid -- particularly balance of payments support -- and faltering production at the copper mines which drive the economy, make conditions extremely tough.

Zambia Consolidated Copper Mines (ZCCM), the country's only real hard-currency earner, has been in the doldrums and some industry analysts believe earnings have fallen 33 percent in the past year compared to 1995.
The country's cash crunch has cut fertilizer imports, and crop yields are forecast sharply down, adding to discontent among the poorest in the 9.5 million population.
The squeeze has also added to rumblings among civil servants angry over the government's failure to pay an increase agreed to last year.

Discontent has also spread among prospective university students. Around 12,000 are eligible for entry this year, but the government says it can only sponsor 1,000, a sure source of resentment among a volatile sector of Zambian society.
Despite its political problems, Chiluba's government has been a darling of the World Bank and the IMF.
The world bodies have resisted pressure from the West to suspend Zambia's programmes, saying the structural adjustment programme was showing success.

The privatisation programme is regarded by some economic analysts as Africa's most successful, with the sale of 130 state firms in four years. Plans to sell off ZCCM are at an advanced stage and bids will be considered next month.
Other firms likely to come under the hammer include those in the telecommunications, chemicals, coal mining, textiles and farming sectors. Income from the sales is difficult to project.

The government has also liberalised trade, scrapped exchange controls and sacked thousands of public servants in an effort to cut spending and boost the economy, which suffered decades of state-ownership and socialist-style planning under Kaunda, who led the country to independence from Britain in 1964.
"Unless something drastic happens in the economy, the IMF and World Bank are unlikely to suspend their programmes here," a Western ambassador told Reuters.
"The multilateral donors badly need an advertisement for structural adjustment and Zambia represents a very good advertisement. They would not like to give it up."
The government is likely to press on with economic reforms crucial for continued multilateral assistance.
Kaunda appears to be betting that increased suffering and possible unrest will unseat the man who took power from him in the country's first democratic elections in 1991.
The former president has predicted that social strife will make the country ungovernable over the next three to six months, but there is little evidence that an uprising is imminent, analysts say.

Zambia's political problems have also led to a cooling of relations with its neighbours, which stuck their necks out in an effort to persuade Chiluba to face the challenge posed by Kaunda, rather than use a heavy hand at the ballot box.
Despite the hiccups, some analysts say the country's prospects are not too bleak and that things can only look up.
They point out that civil strife has not broken out and the economy has carried on despite the aid squeeze.

"Elections are over and it is anticipated that after the presentation of the national budget (on January 31), the economic environment will be conducive to business again," Barclays Bank of Zambia said in a report earlier this month. ($=1,300 kwacha)
